Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verse 1:

Surah al-Mutaffifin

It is also called Surat al-Mutaffifin. There is disagreement over whether it is Meccan or Medinan. According to Ibn Mas'ud and al-Dahhak, it is Meccan; according to al-Hasan and Ikrimah, it is Medinan, and al-Suddi held this view. He said: "There was a man in Medina called Abu Juhayna, who had two measures: he took with the fuller one and gave with the smaller one, so this was revealed."

There are several reports from Ibn Abbas. Ibn al-Durays transmitted from him that he said: "The last surah to be revealed in Mecca was Surat al-Mutaffifin." Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from him that he said: "The first thing revealed in Medina was: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾." This report is supported by what al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, with a sound chain, and others transmitted from him, that he said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were among the worst of people in measuring, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾, and afterwards they measured well." In another report from him and from Qatadah, it is Meccan except for its last eight verses, from ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ onward. It has also been said that it is Medinan except for its first six verses.

Some who recognize an intermediate category between Meccan and Medinan say that it is neither of the two, but was revealed between Mecca and Medina so that Allah the Exalted might set right the affairs of the people of Medina before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived among them. Its number of verses is thirty-six, without disagreement. Its connection to what precedes it is that when Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned earlier the happy and the wretched and the Day of Recompense and its great significance, He mentioned here what He has prepared for some of the disobedient, and described the most contemptible of sins, which is fraud in measure, which hardly benefits in increasing and growing wealth; and this surah, in describing the state of the deniers mentioned there, includes further detail, as is not hidden.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: The placement of this surah between al-Infitar and al-Inshiqaq, which are its counterparts in several respects, is for a subtle reason which Allah the Exalted inspired in me. That is: the four surahs (this one, the two before it, and al-Inshiqaq), since they describe the state of the Day of Resurrection, were mentioned according to the order of what occurs in it. Most of what occurs in al-Takwir and all of what occurs in al-Infitar occurs at the beginning of the Day of Resurrection. After that comes the long standing and the suffering of terrors, which He mentioned in this surah with His saying: ﴿The Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾. After that the Great Intercession occurs, then the scrolls are spread out, one taking with the right hand, another with the left, and another behind his back. After that the reckoning takes place, as the reports indicate. Thus it is fitting that al-Inshiqaq, in which the books are given and the reckoning occurs, comes later than the surah in which the standing is mentioned, and that the surah in which the standing is mentioned comes later than the surah in which the beginnings of the day's states are mentioned. Another aspect: when He, majestic is His majesty, said in al-Infitar: ﴿And indeed over you are guardians, noble writers﴾, which was in the world, He mentioned in this surah what the guardians record, and it is an inscribed register placed in 'Illiyyin or Sijjin; this too is in the world, as the reports indicate. So this is a second state of the book, mentioned in the second surah. It has a third state, later than these two: its being given to its owner with the right hand or otherwise, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. Thus it is fitting that the surah in which that is mentioned comes after the surah in which the second state is mentioned. End of quotation. And although it is not devoid of subtlety, there is room for examination in it, so reflect.

Page 68

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾. It has been said: al-Wayl is extreme evil; it has been said: grief and destruction; it has been said: a painful punishment.

It has also been said: it is a mountain in Hell. This was transmitted from Uthman as a marfu' report by Ibn Jarir with a chain in which there is scrutiny. Many have held that it is a valley in Hell.

For al-Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi transmitted from Abu Sa'id, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Wayl is a valley in Hell, into which the disbeliever will plunge for forty autumns before he reaches its bottom.'"

In the Sahih of Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, with the wording: "a valley between two mountains into which the disbeliever will plunge," and so on. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abd Allah that it is a valley in Hell of pus. In the book al-Mufradat by al-Raghib, al-Asma'i said: wayl is ugliness, and it may be used to express regret. As for the one who says wayl is a valley in Hell, he does not mean that wayl in the language is set for this; rather, he means that whoever Allah the Exalted has described with it has deserved a place in the Fire, and this is established for him. End of quotation.

It appears that its application to that is like its application of Jahannam to what is well known as Hell; so consider from what kind that application is. In any case, it is a subject (mubtada'), and although it is indefinite, it occurs in the position of supplication, and "lil-mutaffifin" is its predicate. Al-tatfif is cheating in measure and weight, because what is cheated in a single measure or weight is a slight thing (tafif), that is, a small, paltry amount. The form tafʿil here is for transitivity or for intensification, and it does not contradict its being from tafif in the stated sense, because the frequency of the act is by the frequency of its occurrence, and it occurs through repetition, not through the abundance of its object. From al-Zajjaj: it is from tafa al-shay', meaning he went to its side.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾ etc. It is a qualifying description (sifah mukhassisah) specifying the defrauders (al-mutaffifin) concerning whom the verse was revealed, or a disclosing description (sifah kashifah) clarifying their condition and explaining the manner of their cheating (tatfif) for which they deserved woe (al-waylu). That is: when they take from people what they take by way of sale or the like, by measure, so that they receive it full and abundant. The replacement of "ʿala" (upon) here with "min" (from) has been said to be for the purpose of implying (tadmin) the sense of seizing (al-istila') in "iktiyal" (taking by measure), or to indicate that it is a measuring that harms people, not in the sense of harm considered from the condition contained in "idha" (when), since that would disrupt the meaning, but in reality, by the requirement of the answer (the apodosis), on the basis that what is meant by "istifa'" (receiving in full) is not taking one's right fully without deficiency, but merely taking abundantly and fully as they wish, by any means available among the stratagems, and they used to do it by packing the measured goods and shaking the measure, and other such things. It has also been said: this is in consideration that their measuring is of what they have as a right upon people. Al-Farra' said that "min" and "ʿala" alternate in this context, so one says "iktaltu ʿalayhi," meaning I took what was upon him by measure, and "iktaltu minhu," meaning I received from him a full measure. This was criticized on the grounds that, although it entails that the ruling does not cover their measuring before they had any claim upon people by way of purchase or the like, which is common among them, it requires that "istifa'" mean taking what is theirs from people in full without deficiency, since that is what is understood from it when used absolutely in the context of a right; thus it would not be the basis for their blame and the invocation of woe against them. Interpreting what is theirs upon them as what will be theirs upon them is very remote and would be of no benefit, for considering that the measured goods belong to them, whether presently or eventually, necessarily requires that "istifa'" have the aforementioned meaning. End of quotation.

I say: Setting aside the question of whether the verse was revealed concerning defrauders whose manner is taking the measured goods of people in full as they wish, there is no harm in interpreting it as indicating that what is taken is a right, presently or eventually. That what is understood from "istifa'" in that case is taking their own property in full without deficiency is granted, but his statement "thus it would not be the basis for their blame and the invocation of woe against them" does no harm. We say: the basis of blame is what is contained in the combination of the two conjoined clauses, as in your saying: "So-and-so takes his right from people in full and gives them their right deficient," which is a common expression for blame. Indeed, blame expressed this way is more severe than blame expressed as "he takes deficient and gives deficient." That it falls short of blame expressed as "he takes excess and gives deficient" does no harm, as is not hidden. Then it may be said: the most common case in measuring by one person from another is that the measured goods are his right in some respect, and perhaps Al-Farra's statement is based on this, so consider it carefully.

It has been permitted that "ʿala" be connected to ﴿yastawfun﴾ (they receive in full), and its placement before the verb serves to convey exclusivity: that is, they receive in full from people specifically, but as for themselves, they receive for themselves. It was criticized on the grounds that restriction by fronting a prepositional phrase occurs only where the verb can also be connected to what is not the prepositional object in the same way it is connected to it, so that by the fronting one intends to restrict it to that object by way of reversal (qalb), or specification (ifrad), or determination (ta'yin), as the context requires. There is no doubt that "istifa'," which is an expression for taking in full, cannot be conceived as being upon themselves, so as for fronting the prepositional phrase to restrict it to people. Moreover, the discourse concerns the act itself, not what the act falls upon. End of quotation.

It was answered: what is meant by "istifa'" when followed by "ʿala" is that harm. So it is as if it were said: when they measure, they harm people specifically and do not harm themselves, but rather benefit themselves. Restriction by way of reversal and harm may apply to themselves just as it may apply to people, although what causes the harm differs: their harming themselves is by taking less, and their harming people is by taking more. Furthermore, the specificity of the object upon which the act falls is the basis of the blame and the invocation of woe, and with this the objection in the additional clause is answered. End of quotation.

But what is in it is not hidden. So reflect.

The personal pronoun in His saying ﴿and when they measure for them or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ refers to the people, and what preceded concerns taking from people, whereas this concerns giving. The meaning is: when they measure out for them or weigh out for them for sale, they diminish. The verb *kāla* (to measure) is used with the object of measure both with the preposition *lām* (for) and without it. It has been said that in the lexicon *kāla lahu* and *kālahu* both mean *kāla lahu*. Many scholars held that *kālahu* is an instance of omission and transmission (*ḥadhf wa-īṣāl*), the original being *kāla lahu*, so the preposition was dropped and the verb was made to take the object directly, as in the verse of the poet:

*"Indeed I gathered for you truffles and wild asparagus,*
*and indeed I forbade you from the daughters of al-Awbar."*

Also their saying in the proverb: "The greedy one hunts for you, not the generous one" — meaning: "he gathers for you" and "he hunts for you."

It is also permissible that the speech is by omission of a modified noun (*muḍāf*), which is "measured goods" (*makīl*) and "weighed goods" (*mawzūn*), with the modified noun put in its place. The original would be: "when they measure out their measured goods, or weigh out their weighed goods."

From ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ḥamza it is reported that the object of measuring and weighing (*al-makīl lahu* and *al-mawzūn lahu*) is omitted, and *hum* is a nominative pronoun for emphasis of the nominative pronoun, which is the *wāw*. They used to pause on the two *wāws* with a brief pause, by which they would make clear what they intended.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is not valid for the pronoun to be nominative referring to the defrauders (*al-muṭaffifīn*), because the meaning would then be: when they take from people, they take their full due; and when they themselves undertake the measuring or weighing, they cause loss specifically. This is an incongruous statement, because the discourse is about the act, not about the one who directly performs it. This is according to what is in *al-Kashf*. For emphasis by repetition of the word (*al-ta'kīd al-lafẓī*) is ruled out by the context, since the aim is not to affirm that the measuring came from them and not from their slaves, for example. Emphasis alone is ruled out by the omission of the *fā'* (*fa*) in the response of *idhā* (when), because the eloquent form in that case would be: "so they cause loss." Thus the restriction (*al-taḫṣīṣ*) is required, and the excuse for omitting the *fā'* appears, since the meaning is that none causes loss except them. Incongruity and loss of the correspondence (*al-muqābala*) follow. This is a first error in ﴿kālūhum﴾, which is an absolute barrier against this estimate. Interpreting it as an omission of the predicate from one of the two parts, namely the half of the conditional, has no parallel. It has also been said that it is unlikely for the pronoun to be nominative because the *alif* is not written after the *wāw*. It is established in the science of orthography that it is written after the *wāw* in such cases, and the ʿUthmānic Qur'anic codex followed this in its parallels. Its being specifically unwritten here, contrary to what is established and to what was followed in the parallels, is far-fetched, as is not hidden.

Perhaps the limitation of the verb to "taking full measure" in the case of receiving, and the mention of measuring and weighing in the case of causing loss, is because the defrauders did not take what is measured and weighed except by measures, not by scales, since they were able to take full measure and steal by measuring. When they gave, they measured and weighed, since they were able to cheat in both kinds together. The conclusion is that the sublime composition came in this form only to correspond to those about whom it was revealed, so that the attribute censures them for their excessive cheating and injustice. This is correct, whether the attribute is made to specify these defrauders, as is most apparent, or is revealing of their condition. The first intends a known mental referent (*maʿhūd dhihnī*).

Our shaykh of shaykhs, the scholar Sayyid Ṣibghat Allāh al-Ḥaydarī, said regarding this: Cheating in measuring occurs with a small amount that is generally not regarded, unlike cheating in weighing, for even the slightest trick in it leads to a great deal. Also, what is weighed is generally more valuable than what is measured. So when the verse informs that they do not spare people even a small, contemptible portion of their rights, it is known that they do not spare them a great amount that most people, indeed people of honour, do not overlook except rarely, all the more so. This is unlike when it is mentioned that they cause people loss in individual items, as is understood from the mention of causing loss in measuring, for it is not known from it that they cause them loss even in a large amount. Indeed, the restriction of the mention to individual items may suggest that they do not dare to cause them loss in the totality of wealth. Therefore the second part must also mention causing loss in weighing, so that the verse proclaims their blameworthy deeds and censures them for their shameful conditions. End of quotation.

It was objected that the question is not settled, because it may be asked: why did He not say "when they take full measure from people, they give full measure, and when they weigh for them, they cause loss," so that from the two clauses it would be known that they take full measure of the large amount and cause loss in the small, contemptible amount, a fortiori, and there would be in the speech what is of the type of *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which each of two parts omits what the other mentions). Al-Zajjāj said: The meaning is: when they measure out from people, they take full measure from them; likewise when they weigh out from people, they take full weight. He did not mention "when they weigh out" because measuring and weighing are both what buying and selling involve in what is measured and weighed. His meaning, as al-Ṭībī explicitly stated, is that he dispensed with mentioning one of the two clauses in favour of the other, because the following clause indicates it. This, as you see, is not satisfactory.

It has also been said that the defrauders were merchants, and they generally buy a large amount at once and then sell it in portions, in installments. How often have we seen among them one who buys from farmers a large quantity of grain, for example, in a single day, and stores it and then sells it bit by bit over many days. Since the prevailing custom is taking a large amount by measure, the mention of "taking full measure" alone is made in the case of receiving. Since what they sell varies in quantity and amount, measuring and weighing are mentioned in the case of giving. Or, since the choice of what determines the quantity is left to the judgement of the one buying from them, both are mentioned together in that case, for some choose measure and some choose weight. You know that it is not granted without qualification that the prevailing custom is taking a large amount by measure; perhaps it is so in some places and not in others. The people of our city, Madinat al-Salām (Baghdad), today do not measure out or receive by measure at all; their custom is weighing and being weighed in general. The non-mention of the measured or weighed item in the two cases, as many have said, is because the thrust of the discourse is to explain the bad dealing of the defrauders in taking and giving, not the specific nature of what is taken or given.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verses 4–5:

﴿Do those not think that they will be resurrected﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that comes to magnify the enormity of the cheating in measure (al-taṭfif) which they committed. The hamza is for denial and wonder, and "lā" is negating; so "alā" here is not the initial interrogative/alerting particle, but is composed of the interrogative hamza and the negating "lā." The verb "yaẓunn" (think) is in its well-known meaning. "Ulā'ika" (those) is a demonstrative referring to the cheaters (al-muṭaffifīn), and its placement in the position of their pronoun is to signal the basis of the ruling, which is their attribute. For pointing to a thing touches upon it in terms of its being characterized by its attribute, whereas the pronoun does not touch upon the attribute. It also indicates that they are distinguished by that ugly attribute from all other people in the most complete distinction, being placed in the rank of things pointed to with a sensory pointing. And what it contains of the meaning of distance (al-bu'd) is to signal the remoteness of their rank in wickedness and corruption. That is: "Do those described by that shameful, appalling attribute not think that they will be resurrected ﴿for a tremendous day﴾, whose greatness cannot be measured? For whoever thinks that, even if it is a weak thought, hardly dares to commit such abominations, so how about one who is certain of it?" The day was described as "great" because of the greatness of what occurs in it, just as making it the cause of the resurrection is in consideration of what occurs in it. Some have supposed an omitted noun, that is: "for the reckoning of a day." It was also said: "yaẓunn" here means "certainty," but the first is preferable and more eloquent.

It is related from al-Zamakhshari that He, glorified is He, made them worse in condition than the disbelievers, because He affirmed for the disbelievers a "ẓann" (thought) when He related of them: ﴿We only think a thought﴾, and He did not affirm it for them, mighty and majestic is He. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, placed them in the position of one who does not think, so that the denial would be valid.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ — that is, for His judgment and His decree, exalted and mighty is He — is in the accusative by an implied verb, "I mean" (a'ni). It is also permissible that it be an object of "resurrected" (mab'uthun), or in the nominative position as the predicate of an implied subject: i.e., "it is," or "that is a day"; or in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for "a mighty day," as al-Farra' said. On both of these two readings it is built on the fatha because it is attached to a verb, even though the verb is imperfect, as is the view of the Kufans, and this has been mentioned more than once. The two readings are supported by the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali: "yawmun" in the nominative, and the reading of some others, as Abu Mu'adh related: "yawmi" in the genitive. In this there is denial, astonishment, the introduction of suspicion (zann), the use of the demonstrative, and describing the day of their standing with greatness; and [there is] the substitution of "the day when they stand" etc. from it, on the view that it is a substitute, and its description by the Lordship of the worlds, [which is] from the eloquent exposition of the greatness of the sin and the magnitude of the wrong in cheating (taṭfif), which is not hidden. This is not with regard to cheating as such, insofar as it is cheating, but rather insofar as the balance is the law of justice by which the heavens and the earth stand; so the ruling encompasses cheating in the manner that those cheaters committed it, and other than it.

It is authentically transmitted, from the narration of al-Hakim, al-Tabarani and others, from Ibn 'Abbas and others, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Five for five." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is 'five for five'?" He said: "No people break a covenant except that Allah, exalted is He, gives their enemy power over them; they do not rule by other than what Allah has sent down except that poverty spreads among them; immorality does not appear among them except that death spreads among them; they do not cheat in measure except that they are denied vegetation and are seized by years of drought; and they do not withhold zakat except that rain is held back from them."

And from Ibn 'Umar that he would pass by a seller and say: "Fear Allah, exalted is He, and give full measure; for the cheaters will be held on the Day of Resurrection before the greatness of the Merciful, to the point that sweat will bridle them." And from 'Ikrimah: "I testify that every measurer and weigher is in the Fire." It was said to him: "Your son is a measurer and weigher." He said: "I testify that he is in the Fire." It seems he intended exaggeration, knowing that cheating was prevalent among them. Of this kind is what is related from Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do not seek needs from one whose provision is at the heads of measures and the tongues of scales." And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

It has been cited, with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when they stand﴾ etc., as evidence against standing up for people, since it is specific to Allah, exalted is He. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti answered it by saying that it is specific to standing for a man before whom one stands, but as for standing for him when he arrives and then sitting, that is not forbidden. And you know that the verse is far from being cited as evidence for what has been mentioned, such that it would need this answer; and I consider citing it for that to be a strange and remarkable thing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verse 7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay﴾ is a deterrent from what they were upon of defrauding (al-tatfif) and heedlessness of the Resurrection and the Reckoning. ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ etc. It is a cause (ta'lil) for the deterrent, or for the obligation of restraint (al-irtida'), by way of affirmation (al-tahqiq). As for "kitab" (record), it has been said to mean "maktub" (written), i.e., what is written of the deeds of the wicked: ﴿is in﴾ etc. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning "writing," and in the statement there is an implied genitive construction (mudaf muqaddar), i.e., the writing of the deeds of the wicked is in etc. ...

The intended meaning of ﴿the wicked﴾ (al-fujjar) here, according to what Abu Hayyan said, is the disbelievers. According to what many others said, it includes them and the grossly sinful (al-fasaqah), so the defrauders enter among them. As for "Sijjin," it has been said to be an adjective on the pattern of "sikkir" (one who is very drunk/intoxicated, an intensive form). Many others have chosen that it is a proper name (alam) for a comprehensive register, which is the register of evil, in which the deeds of the corrupt from both groups (jinn and humankind) are recorded, as God, Exalted is He, said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verses 8–9:

﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record, inscribed.﴾ The apparent view is that "kitab" (a written record) is an apposition (badal) to "sijjin," or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada') which is a pronoun referring back to it, meaning: "It is a written record." Its original sense is a descriptive adjective derived from "al-sajn" (imprisonment) with the vowel of the sin pronounced as a fatha. The record was given this name because it is the cause of confinement. Thus, originally, it is of the pattern "fa'il" in the sense of "fa'il" (active participle), or it is named so because, as is said, it is cast beneath the earths in a desolate place, as if it were imprisoned, so it carries the sense of "maf'ul" (passive participle). Making it a proper name for the reason mentioned does not entail that the record is a container for the record, since you have heard the explanation of "the record of the wicked." Accordingly, the record mentioned would be a container for the deed that is written in it, or a container for the writing. It has also been said: the "record" is in its literal sense, and the statement is like your saying: "The record of the calculation of such-and-such village is in such-and-such register, since it contains its calculation and the calculation of its like," in that the containment in it is the containment of the whole in the part. And from the Imam (al-Razi): there is no improbability in one of the two being placed within the other literally, or the content of one being transferred to the other. And from Ubayy (ibn Ka'b), on the reading that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a written record, inscribed﴾ means: "the place of a record," so "kitab" is in its literal sense, and "sijjin" is a place in his view. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, al-Falaq is a well in Hell, covered, and Sijjin is a well in it, open."

Accordingly, Sijjin is the worst place in Hell. Reports in several narrations state that it is a place beneath the seventh earth, and there is no contradiction between this and the aforementioned report, based on the view that Hell is beneath the earth. In al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari): it is not improbable that "Sijjin" is both the name of the record and the name of the place, combining the apparent meaning of the verse with the apparent meanings of the reports. Some of those who held that in the verse it is the name of a place said: "And what will make you know Sijjin?" with an omitted genitive construction (mudaf), meaning: "And what will make you know what the record of Sijjin is?" Ibn 'Atiyya said: whoever holds this view, then "kitab" in his view is in the nominative as the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and the adverbial phrase (zarf) which is ﴿indeed in Sijjin﴾ is cancelled (mulgha). The words of Him, exalted is He: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ are connected to His words: ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical digression (i'tiraDh). The meaning is: woe to those who deny that day. As for His words: ﴿who deny the Day of Judgment﴾, it may be in the genitive (majrur) as a vituperative qualifier (sifah dhammah, an adjective expressing blame) of "the deniers," or an apposition (badal) to it, or in the nominative (marfu') or accusative (mansub) by way of censure (dhamm). It is also permissible for it to be a clarifying, explanatory qualifier (sifah kashifah muwaddihah). It has been said that it is a distinguishing, specifying qualifier (sifah mukhassisah farigah), meaning that the intended referent is those who deny the truth. But the first view is more apparent, because His words: ﴿And none deny it except every transgressor﴾ ... etc. indicate that the intention is censure. That is: none deny the Day of Judgment except every one who exceeds the bounds of reflection and consideration, who is excessive in blind imitation (taqlid), to the extent that he makes God's power fall short of restoration and His knowledge fall short of knowing the scattered parts which are necessary for restoration. Thus he deems restoration impossible for Him, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿Sinful﴾, i.e., one who commits many sins, immersed in the base and transient desires, so that they have preoccupied him from what lies beyond them of complete and lasting delights, and have driven him to deny them. ﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, which express this, ﴿he says﴾, out of extreme ignorance and turning away from the truth from which there is no escape: ﴿"Tales of the ancients."﴾ That is: they are the stories of the ancients, meaning they are falsehoods brought by the earlier people, and the time since they were reported has grown long while their truth has not become evident; or they are falsehoods that were cast upon our ancient forefathers, who denied them, and we are not the first to deny them, so that denial by us would be hasty and a departure from the path of prudence and caution. The first view is more apparent.

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith; and on the authority of al-Kalbi, that it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Whichever it was, the statement is general in application. Abu Haywah and Ibn Muqsim read ﴿idha yutla﴾ with the verb in the masculine form, and it has also been read ﴿a-idha tutla﴾ as a rhetorical interrogative of denial.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verse 14:

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke to the transgressor, the sinner, for that false saying, and a denial of it. His words, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Nay, but what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾ are an explanation of what led them to utter that monstrous statement. That is: there is nothing in Our verses that would justify saying about them such a false statement. Rather, ("rana") covered their hearts and overpowered them, the sin they persisted in earning, of disbelief and disobedience, until it became like rust on a mirror, and this barred them from recognizing the truth. Therefore they said what they said. And ar-rain (rust) in origin means rust. It is said: "ran" the sin over him (ra'a 'alayhi al-dhanb), and "ghan" (ghana 'alayhi) raynan and ghaynan. It is also said: "ran" sleep upon him, that is, it settled firmly in him. In al-Bahr: the origin of ar-rayn is domination. It is said: wine "ranat" over the mind of its drinker, that is, it overcame it; and faintness "ran" over the mind of the sick person, that is, it overcame it. Abu Zayd said: it is said, "rīna bi-l-rajul yurānu bihi raynan" when a man falls into something from which he cannot escape. What is meant by it is the firmly rooted love of sins, by the common quality that it is like the rust that blackens a mirror or silver, for example, altering it from its original state.

And Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed, when a servant commits a sin, a black spot is inscribed upon his heart. If he repents, withdraws and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished; but if he returns to it, the spot increases until it covers his heart."

That is the ran (rust) which Allah Almighty mentioned in the Qur'an: ﴿Nay, but what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They used to think that ar-rayn is the sealing (tab')," and they mentioned causes for it.

In a hadith narrated by 'Abd ibn Humayd through the chain of Khulayd ibn al-Hakam, from Abu al-Mujbar: "He (peace be upon him) said: Four qualities corrupt the hearts: keeping company with the fool, for if you associate with him you become like him, and if you remain silent about him you are safe from him; excessive sins, which corrupt the hearts, and Allah Almighty has said: ﴿Nay, but what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾; seclusion with women, enjoying them, and acting upon their opinion; and sitting with the dead." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they?" He said: "Every rich man whose wealth has made him insolent."

It has been recited with idgham of the lam into the ra' (in bal ran). Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Badhish said: "The reciters agreed upon idgham of the lam into the ra', except for Hafs's pause on bal with a light, slight pause to clarify the izhar (clear pronunciation)." But this is not as he claimed regarding consensus, for in al-Lawami' it is narrated from Qalun, through all his routes, that the lam is made clear (izhar) before the ra', as in His words: ﴿Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ and ﴿Nay, your Lord is...﴾. In Ibn 'Atiyyah's book it says: Nafi' recited ﴿bal ran﴾ without idgham, and also in it: Nafi' also recited with idgham and imalah. Sibawayh said regarding the lam with the ra', as in ash-ghala ra-hmahu: the clear pronunciation (bayan) and the idgham are both good. He also said: when the lam is not the lam of definiteness, such as the lam in hal and bal, idgham is better; if it is not assimilated, it is a dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and it is a permissible Arabic usage. In al-Kashshaf: it has been recited with idgham of the lam into the ra', and with izhar; idgham is better, and the alif was given imalah and tafkhim (emphasis). So let this be noted.

﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke and a deterrent from the sinful earning (al-kasb al-rayn, the earning that stains the heart with sin), or it means "truly." ﴿Indeed they﴾, namely these deniers, ﴿on that Day, from their Lord, will be veiled﴾, meaning they will not see Him, glory be to Him, whereas He, mighty and majestic, is present and watching over them. This is unlike the believers. So "veiling" is a metaphor for not seeing, because one who is veiled does not see what is veiled from him. Or "veiling" means prevention, and the speech contains an elided noun: that is, they will be prevented from seeing their Lord, so they will not see Him, glory be to Him. Malik used this verse as evidence that the believers will see Him, exalted is He, by way of dalil al-khitab (the argument from implication, where the restriction in a text implies its opposite for what is not mentioned). Otherwise, if all were veiled, this specification would serve no purpose.

Al-Shafi'i said: Since He, glory be to Him, veiled one people through wrath, this indicates that another people will see Him through good pleasure. Anas ibn Malik said: When He, mighty and majestic, veiled His enemies, glory be to Him, so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself, exalted is His majesty, to His friends until they saw Him, mighty and majestic. As for one who denies His seeing, exalted is He, such as the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), they say: The speech is an illustration of contempt for them and their humiliation, because access to kings is not granted except to the dignitaries honored in their presence, and none is veiled from them except the lowly who are despised in their sight, as the poet said:

When they come to the gate of one with pride, they are kept waiting,
and people are divided between one who is admitted and one who is kept out.

Or it is with an elided noun: that is, they are veiled from the mercy of their Lord, for example. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Mujahid related this estimation. Ibn Kaysan related the estimation of "honor," but they intended the generality of what is elided, covering the vision and other of His graces, exalted is He. The prepositional phrase ﴿from their Lord﴾ is related to "veiled," and it is the governing element for ﴿on that Day﴾. The nunation in "that Day" (yawma'idhin) is nunation of compensation, and what is compensated for here is the preceding "the people stand," as if it were said: Indeed they will be veiled from their Lord on the Day when the people stand before the Lord of the worlds.

Verse 16: "Then indeed they will be those who burn in the Hellfire" (﴿ثُمَّ إنَّهم لَصالُو الجَحِيمِ﴾).

"Burning in it" means: enduring its heat, according to what al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi, the lexicographer) said. It was also said: they will be entering it (dakhiluna fiha), and "then" (thumma) was said to indicate a distance in rank, but this is based on their own view, for the burning of the Fire, in their estimation, is more severe than their being veiled from their Lord, Mighty and Majestic is He. As for the believers, especially those among them who are enraptured with love for Him, glory be to Him, the veil is a torment to which no other torment comes close.

Then it will be said [to them], as a rebuke and reproach, from the direction of the guardians (al-khazana) or the people of Paradise: ﴿This is what you used to deny.﴾

Indeed, the record of the wicked...﴾ and so on, so that it is followed by the promise for the righteous, just as that was followed by the threat against the wicked. This signals that cheating in measure is wickedness and fulfilling the measure is righteousness. It is also said that it is a deterrence from denial, and so there is no repetition.

﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin.﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what ʿIlliyyun is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ The discourse is similar to what has passed concerning its counterpart, except that they differed about ﴿ʿIlliyyin﴾ on a different basis from their difference concerning (Sijjin). Many said: it is a proper name for the register in which everything done by the angels and the righteous of the two weighty things (jinn and humankind) is recorded. It is derived from the plural on the pattern faʿīl from ʿuluww (height), like Sijjīn from al-sajn (imprisonment). It was so named either because it is the means of ascent to the high ranks of the Gardens, or because it is raised in the seventh heaven, or near the right pillar of the Throne, along with the nearest angels, and the name was given to it to honour it.

It is also said that it refers to the lofty places, whose singular is ʿAliyy. The expected form would be ʿiliyyah, as they say ʿiliyyah for an upper room, but when they dropped the tā’, they compensated for it with the plural suffix of the masculine sound plural (-ūn/-īn). This is reported from Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni. It is also said that it is a description of the angels, and for that reason it takes the masculine sound plural. Al-Farra’ said: it is a noun formed on the pattern of the plural, with no singular from its own form, like ʿishrūn (twenty) and thalāthūn (thirty). When the Arabs form a plural that has no singular pattern and no dual, they apply it to both masculine and feminine with the masculine sound plural suffix.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 83, verses 25–26:**

﴿They are given to drink of a pure wine (raḥīq)﴾. Al-Khalil said: it is the finest of wine. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said: it is the drink that has no adulteration in it. Hassan said:

*They give to drink to whoever comes to al-Bariṣ, while on them is Barada, poured with pure, smooth raḥīq.*

Here it is interpreted as the pure drink, unmixed with anything that spoils it, not even the ghawl (the harm that comes from drinking wine). ﴿Sealed﴾ ﴿its seal is musk﴾: meaning, its containers and cups are sealed with musk in place of clay, as narrated from Mujahid. It is mentioned that the clay of Paradise is kneaded musk. The apparent meaning is that the khitām is that with which something is sealed, and that the sealing is in its literal sense, and likewise its attribution. Our statement "its containers are sealed" does not mean that the attribution is figurative, but rather that sealing something, meaning securing it by a seal, follows this manner, and it is sealed out of care for it and to show honor to its drinker. This was done with something in the form of clay so that it would be in the familiar manner. It is also possible that this is a figure of speech for the perfection of its preciousness, since there is no dust, flies, or treachery there that would need to be guarded by a seal.

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan said: the meaning is that its ending (khātimah) and its final part is the scent of musk when it is drunk. That is, the drinker finds that scent at the end of his drinking. This is because the taster's occupation with the full pleasure of the drink prevents him from perceiving the scent, so when drinking stops, he perceives it. Otherwise, the scent is not restricted to the end. It was also said: the meaning is "having an end whose end," and what remains after drinking it, and what is drunk from its vessels, is musk, unlike the drinks of this world, whose end is not like that. And what settles in its vessel is clay or something similar. But this is as you see. It was also said: the raḥīq is mixed with camphor and its mixture is sealed with musk, so the meaning is "having a seal whose seal of its mixture is musk." Although this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and what follows it contains something that generally distances it, it needs a transmission on which one can rely.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Nakha'i, al-Dahhak, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿khātamuhu﴾ with an alif after the kha' and a fatḥah on the tā'. The intended meaning is also what is sealed with it, since fā'il with fatḥah can also be a noun of instrument, like *al-qālab* (mould) and *al-ṭābi'* (stamp), but this is only by transmission (samā'ī). It is narrated from al-Dahhak, Isa and Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, from al-Kisa'i, that the tā' is kasrah; that is, its last part is the scent of musk. The preceding sentences, namely ﴿They recline on couches, looking﴾ and ﴿You will recognize in their faces﴾ etc., and ﴿and they are given to drink﴾ etc., are said to be successive states (aḥwāl mutarādifah). It was also said that they are resumed sentences (mustaʾnafāt), like the sentence ﴿Indeed the righteous﴾ etc., which occurred as answers to a question about their condition. The separation (of the sentences) is to draw attention to the independence of each in explaining their honor.

﴿And for that﴾: a reference to the raḥīq, which is the most suitable for what follows, or to what has been mentioned of their conditions, and in it is the meaning of distance, to indicate the loftiness of its rank and the greatness of its station. It was also permitted that it refers to its being in Paradise. The prepositional phrase is connected to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so let those who compete compete﴾, and it was placed first for emphasis or for restriction; that is: ﴿so let them compete and desire it﴾, not the wines of this world, or not other than its pleasures and blessings. ﴿Those who compete﴾, that is, those who are eager to hasten to the obedience of Allah, may He be exalted. It was also said: that is, let the workers work for its sake; that is, for the sake of attaining it alone and winning it, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾. That is, let those who race strive to attain it.

The root of *tanāfus* is competition for a precious thing, and its root is from *nafs* (self) because of its preciousness. Al-Wahidi said: "I found the thing precious (nafistu al-shay'a nafāsah), and *tanāfus* is a reciprocal form of it, as if one of the two persons wants to monopolize it." Al-Baghawi said: its root is from the precious thing that people's souls covet and that everyone desires for himself. It is said: "I begrudged him the thing (nafistu 'alayhi bi-l-shay')," meaning when you are stingy with it toward him. In al-Raghib's *Mufradat*: *al-munafasah* is the striving of the soul to resemble the virtuous and to catch up with them, without causing harm to others. In this sense it is part of the nobility of the soul and the loftiness of aspiration, and the difference between it and envy (ḥasad) is too clear to be hidden.

This connection has been questioned, because it would entail that a conjunction (fā') comes after a conjunction (wāw), since the estimated reading would be "and let him compete in that." It was answered that it is by estimating a saying; that is, they say, because of the intensity of enjoyment, without choice, about that: ﴿so let those who compete compete﴾; that is, in this world, in the sense that it was fitting for them to compete in that. It was also said: the speech is under the assumption of a conditional particle, and the fā' is in its response; that is, "and if competition is desired, then let those who compete compete for that." The placing of the adverbial phrase first is so that it takes the place of the condition in occupying its position, and it is more precious than what came before.

The truth is that there is no rejection, as is not hidden. The word "tathwib" and "ithaba" means recompense. It is said: "thawwabahu wa-athabahu" when he recompensed him. From this is the poet's saying:

"I will repay you, or a repayer will repay you on my behalf, and it is enough for you that you be praised and commended."

The apparent sense of their words is that this applies to recompense with good and evil, but it is well known for recompense with good, and it is permissible to take it in that sense here, on the basis that the intended meaning is mockery, as has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ and ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾. It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying to the believers: "Have We rewarded these people for what they used to do, just as We rewarded you for what you used to do?" In that case this statement adds to their joy, because of what it contains of honoring them and belittling their enemies. The interrogative clause is then governed by an implied verb of saying which occurs as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (they laugh) or from the pronoun in (they look); that is: they laugh or they look, being told ﴿Have they been rewarded...﴾ etc. The majority did not address this. In al-Bahr: the interrogative is for the affirmation of the believers, and the meaning is: the disbelievers have indeed been recompensed for what they used to do, etc. It has been said: ﴿Have they been rewarded﴾ is connected to ﴿they look﴾, and the clause is in the place of a object of it after dropping the preposition "ila" (to), which is "intaha" (reached), and "ma" is either verbal (maṣdariyya) or relative, with a returning pronoun omitted; that is: they do it. The sentence is with an implied noun; that is: the reward or recompense of what they used to do, etc. It has been said: it is with an implied preposition of causality (ba' al-sababiyya); that is: have the disbelievers been rewarded because of what they used to do. The two Nahwi readers (al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr, i.e. the two grammarians), Hamza and Ibn Muhaysin read with assimilation of the lam into the ta'.

And God Most High knows best.
